Torres del Paine · Chile
The full route

From the Pacific to the Caribbean — and back again.

The map connects the stops in the order you told me the journey happened. The figures are minimum straight-line distances between places — not the actual kilometres travelled by road or air — so the real journey was even longer.

01

Chile

Where everything began

≈ 4,726 km connecting these stops
01
0 km from the previous stop

Santiago de Chile

Founded by Pedro de Valdivia in 1541 beside the Mapocho River, Santiago grew on land inhabited long before the Spanish arrived. It evolved from a colonial settlement into the capital of the republic and eventually into a vast metropolis wedged between the Andes and the Coastal Range.

♡ This is where everything began: kilometre zero of Maud’s Latin American journey.

02
899 km from the previous stop

Puerto Varas

The Llanquihue basin has a much older Indigenous history connected to the Huilliche world. Puerto Varas took shape from 1853 during state-sponsored German colonisation, a legacy still visible in its architecture, gardens and baking traditions.

♡ Lakes, volcanoes, and the first real step into Chile’s deep south.

03
86 km from the previous stop

Tagua Tagua Lake & Park

In the Puelo River basin, Tagua Tagua Lake lies between granite mountains and Valdivian rainforest. Tagua Tagua Park was created in 2013 as a private protected area: 3,000 hectares of conservation, ancient alerce trees, waterfalls and trails reached by crossing the lake.

♡ A remote stop: water, forest, and the feeling of disappearing from the map for a while.

04
1,119 km from the previous stop

Puerto Natales

Puerto Natales developed in the early twentieth century around sheep farming and navigation through Última Esperanza. Today it is the gateway to Torres del Paine, while still feeling like a port town shaped by the Patagonian fjords.

♡ The last base before entering one of the defining landscapes of her journey.

05
107 km from the previous stop + 80 km on foot

Torres del Paine · W Trek

The Paine massif belongs to one of southern Patagonia’s great glacial landscapes. Protected nationally since 1959, the park combines granite towers, lakes, glaciers and steppe. The W Trek covers roughly 70–80 km through some of its most famous valleys.

♡ Days of walking with a home on her back. One of the images that best captures the physical scale of the journey.

06
107 km from the previous stop

Puerto Natales

Back to the port, and from here across the border into Argentina.

♡ The end of the first great Chilean chapter and the beginning of Argentine Patagonia.

30
2,212 km from the previous stop

Santiago de Chile · return

Returning to a city is never returning to the same place: this time Santiago already meant something within the journey.

♡ Skiing, days together, and a city beginning to mean something completely different.

31
98 km from the previous stop

Valparaíso

Valparaíso was one of the great Pacific ports of the nineteenth century, a crucial stop before the Panama Canal opened. Its amphitheatre of hills, funiculars and port architecture preserves the imprint of a cosmopolitan city and was recognised by UNESCO in 2003.

♡ Hills, the Pacific and colour before returning once more to Santiago.

32
98 km from the previous stop

Santiago · departure for Colombia

Another departure from the same point, this time towards the north of the continent.

♡ There was still room on the map.

02

Argentina

Patagonia, city life and great water

≈ 3,346 km connecting these stops
07
155 km from the previous stop

El Calafate

El Calafate began as a supply point for sheep ranches and was officially founded in 1927. Its growth became tied to Los Glaciares National Park and the vast Patagonian Ice Field; today it is the main gateway to Perito Moreno Glacier.

♡ Carnival in Patagonia: a fairly improbable — and perfect — way to begin Argentina.

08
120 km from the previous stop

El Chaltén

The name Chaltén comes from the Tehuelche world and is often interpreted as 'smoking mountain', after the clouds that gather around Fitz Roy. One of Argentina’s youngest towns, it was founded in 1985 in a border context and later became the country’s National Trekking Capital.

♡ One of the places where she stopped merely passing through and decided to stay. Mountains that made time move more slowly.

09
2,022 km from the previous stop

Buenos Aires

Buenos Aires was founded twice, in 1536 and 1580, and its destiny became inseparable from the Río de la Plata. A viceregal capital from 1776 and a major immigration port in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, it became a city of cafés, avenues, politics, tango and a deeply port-oriented identity.

♡ After weeks of trails: a megacity, noise, books, cafés and the Río de la Plata.

11
1,049 km from the previous stop

Iguazú / Iguaçu Falls

El río Iguazú forma aquí un sistema de cataratas de casi tres kilómetros, compartido por Argentina y Brazil. Sus parques nacionales protegen una gran porción de selva atlántica y ambos lados fueron reconocidos por la UNESCO. El nombre deriva del guaraní y suele traducirse como 'agua grande'.

♡ Aquí Maud tocó Brazil por primera vez: dos países separados por agua que cae con una fuerza absurda.

03

Paraguay

Not every stop has to become a favourite

≈ 303 km connecting these stops
12
303 km from the previous stop

Asunción

Asunción was founded in 1537 and quickly became one of the main Spanish centres of the Río de la Plata basin. Expeditions left from here to establish other cities, earning it the nickname 'Mother of Cities'. Its history was also marked by the wars that transformed Paraguay in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.

♡ Not every place has to become a favourite to belong to the story. Paraguay matters too, because a real journey is never just a collection of highlights.

04

Bolivia

The country where passing through became staying

≈ 1,708 km connecting these stops
13
1,014 km from the previous stop

Santa Cruz de la Sierra

Founded in 1561 by Ñuflo de Chávez, Santa Cruz moved several times during its early decades before settling in its present location. From a relatively isolated eastern city, especially during the twentieth century it became one of Bolivia’s demographic and economic engines.

♡ Bolivia began in the east: heat, lowlands, and a country very different from the Altiplano that would come later.

14
86 km from the previous stop

Samaipata

Samaipata is a crossroads of worlds. El Fuerte preserves a vast ceremonial rock shaped by pre-Hispanic societies, later occupied by the Inca, and positioned on a route that would eventually connect Santa Cruz with colonial Andean centres. UNESCO considers it an exceptional testimony to pre-Hispanic traditions.

♡ The second place after El Chaltén where staying became part of the journey rather than a pause from it.

15
173 km from the previous stop

Sucre

Founded as La Plata in 1538 on Yampara territory, Sucre became the judicial, religious and cultural centre of Charcas. Much of the intellectual life surrounding independence developed here, and it remains Bolivia’s constitutional capital. Its historic centre blends European architecture with local traditions.

♡ Three weeks learning Spanish: a city that also became a classroom.

16
204 km from the previous stop

Cochabamba

The Cochabamba valley has been an important agricultural zone since pre-Hispanic times. The colonial city developed as Villa de Oropesa in the sixteenth century and for centuries served as a breadbasket and connector of Bolivia’s central valleys.

♡ A transition between valleys and the Altiplano; Bolivia changing landscape once again.

17
231 km from the previous stop

La Paz

Nuestra Señora de La Paz was founded in 1548 and soon moved to the valley of Chuquiago Marka. Its extreme vertical geography makes it one of the world’s most distinctive urban capitals; since the late nineteenth century it has been the seat of Bolivia’s government.

♡ The end of Bolivia. And the place where she got to know someone special very well.

05

Peru

Inca paths, desert and mountains

≈ 2,351 km connecting these stops
18
528 km from the previous stop

Cusco

Cusco was the great political and ceremonial centre of the Tahuantinsuyo. After the conquest, the Spanish built churches and mansions over Inca walls, leaving a city where two urban worlds remain visible at the same time.

♡ She arrived earlier than planned because of an emergency in the country — and the journey began by sharing a plane with me.

19
75 km from the previous stop + 43 km on foot

Inca Trail → Machu Picchu

The Inca Trail follows a network of paths, stairways and archaeological sites connected to the Andean road system. Machu Picchu, built in the fifteenth century between the Andes and the Amazon basin, is one of the most extraordinary architectural and landscape legacies of the Inca civilisation.

♡ Arriving on foot changes the scale of Machu Picchu: before the postcard came days of trail.

20
377 km from the previous stop

Arequipa

Founded by the Spanish in 1540 in a valley inhabited long before, Arequipa developed a distinctive architectural identity in white and pink volcanic sillar. Its mestizo baroque style combines European forms with Indigenous craftsmanship in a city repeatedly shaped by earthquakes.

♡ Volcanoes, sillar and another kind of Andean city.

21
404 km from the previous stop

Nazca

Across the desert around Nasca and Palpa stretch hundreds of lines and geoglyphs made roughly between 500 BCE and 500 CE. Animals, plants and enormous geometric figures still form one of the continent’s most enigmatic archaeological landscapes.

♡ After the mountains, the desert began writing the journey in lines.

22
180 km from the previous stop

Paracas

Paracas gives its name both to an important pre-Hispanic culture of Peru’s southern coast and to a peninsula rich in marine life. The National Reserve, created in 1975, protects coastal desert, islands and Pacific waters in one of the starkest meetings of sand and ocean.

♡ A couple of days where the desert literally ends in the sea.

23
217 km from the previous stop

Lima

Fundada en 1535 como Ciudad de los Reyes, Lima fue durante siglos la capital política, religiosa y económica del Virreinato del Peru. Terremotos y transformaciones urbanas cambiaron mucho la ciudad, pero su centro histórico conserva la huella de aquel poder colonial.

♡ The coast turned capital; a pause before climbing back into the Andes.

24
285 km from the previous stop

Huaraz

Huaraz lies at the foot of the Cordillera Blanca in a valley inhabited by Andean societies long before colonial rule. The 1970 earthquake destroyed much of the modern city; rebuilt afterwards, it is now the main base for exploring some of the world’s highest tropical peaks.

♡ Mountains again. The journey seemed to be leaving the Andes, and the Andes kept calling her back.

25
285 km from the previous stop

Lima · regreso

Regreso a Lima para cerrar Peru y tomar uno de los grandes saltos del viaje: atravesar el continente hasta Río.

♡ La última parada peruana antes de encontrarnos en Brazil.

06

Brazil

The chapter we shared

≈ 4,628 km connecting these stops
26
3,779 km from the previous stop

Rio de Janeiro

Fundada en 1565, Río fue puerto colonial, capital del imperio portugués trasladado a América en 1808 y capital de Brazil hasta 1960. Montañas, bahías y playas forman un paisaje urbano tan particular que la UNESCO lo reconoció como paisaje cultural.

♡ Rio was not just another stop: this part of the journey was ours together.

27
127 km from the previous stop

Brazilian Coast

Between Rio and São Paulo, the Atlantic coast brings together old ports, caiçara communities, islands and remnants of Atlantic Forest. For centuries it was a maritime corridor; today it is a road of beaches and towns between two of South America’s largest cities.

♡ Moving down the coast, making the road between cities part of the destination.

28
233 km from the previous stop

São Paulo

São Paulo nació en 1554 alrededor de una misión jesuita. El café, el ferrocarril, la inmigración y luego la industrialización convirtieron aquella pequeña población del planalto en la mayor metrópolis de Brazil.

♡ After jungle, sea and mountains: a city that seems never to end.

29
489 km from the previous stop

Florianópolis

The history of Florianópolis is tied to Santa Catarina Island, Indigenous peoples and strong Azorean migration from the eighteenth century onward. Its identity combines fortifications, fishing villages, lagoons, dunes and a modern city stretching between island and mainland.

♡ El último Brazil antes de tomar un avión de vuelta a Santiago.

07

Colombia

The plan changed; the journey continued

≈ 5,181 km connecting these stops
33
4,258 km from the previous stop

Bogotá

Bogotá rose on the Muisca high plateau and was founded as a Spanish city in 1538. Over time it became a viceregal and republican capital, and eventually a vast Andean metropolis more than 2,600 metres above sea level.

♡ Her arrival coincided with a presidential transition for which the city was preparing with demonstrations and preventive measures. In the end, what actually changed the itinerary was the August 2026 earthquake.

34
715 km from the previous stop

Minca

Minca lies on the slopes of the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, an isolated mountain system and ancestral territory of Indigenous peoples of the Sierra. Coffee estates developed here in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries; today it remains a green, cooler refuge above the Caribbean.

♡ The Caribbean heat became so intense that the only answer was to climb into the mountains and breathe.

35
24 km from the previous stop + 44 km on foot

Ciudad Perdida · Lost City Trek

Teyuna, known as the Lost City, was built by Tairona communities centuries before the Spanish arrived. Its stone terraces, paths and plazas are hidden in the Sierra Nevada, and reaching it today requires several days of trekking through jungle and rivers.

♡ Once again, the destination had to be earned on foot: the jungle took over from Patagonia and the Andes.

36
184 km from the previous stop

Cartagena de Indias

Founded in 1533, Cartagena became one of the Spanish empire’s most important fortified Caribbean ports. Its walls and fortresses recall centuries of trade, sieges, slavery and Atlantic exchange; its monumental complex is a World Heritage Site.

♡ The Caribbean as the final page before the flight back.

37
0 km from the previous stop

Cartagena → Santiago

From here, the journey returns to Chile.

♡ And in Santiago, a surprise is waiting for her.

Uruguay

A detour across the Río de la Plata

≈ 205 km connecting these stops
10
205 km from the previous stop

Uruguay · bonus track

Across the Río de la Plata, Uruguay emerged from a region contested for centuries by the Spanish and Portuguese crowns. Places such as Colonia del Sacramento and Montevideo preserve that history of frontier, port and Atlantic exchange.

♡ A small detour on the map before turning north again. The journey’s bonus track.

Last stop, for now

Santiago.

Where the surprise is waiting. ♡

After more than 27,516 minimum mapped kilometres, the route comes back to the country where it began. The story does not end here; it simply reaches a page that has not been written yet.

To be continued…
